Paragraph:
Translation: For the soul there is never birth nor death. Nor, having once been, does he ever cease to be. He is unborn, eternal, ever-existing, undying and primeval. He is not slain when the body is slain.

Purport (Excerpt): Qualitatively, the small atomic fragmental part of the Supreme Spirit is one with the Supreme. He undergoes no changes like the body. Sometimes the soul is called the steady, or kutastha. The body is subject to six kinds of transformations. It takes its birth... grows... dwindles, and at last vanishes... The soul, however, does not go through such changes.
Situation/Problem_Faced: Arjuna needs a comprehensive summary of the soul's nature to fully counteract his fear of death and bodily changes.
Key_Teaching/Action_Taken: Krishna provides a definitive, poetic summary of the soul's attributes: unborn, eternal, undying, and primeval. He explicitly contrasts this with the six transformations of the physical body (birth, growth, dwindling, death, etc.).
Outcome/Resolution: Arjuna is given a clear, immovable anchor of absolute reality to hold onto amidst the chaos of the battlefield and physical life.

Mental_Health_Theme_Synonyms.core Identity: The unchanging essence of a person
Mental_Health_Theme_Synonyms.transcendence: Rising above physical limitations and fears

Spiritual_Psychological_Concept_Indian.Concept: Sad-vikara (The six transformations of the material body, from which the soul is free)

Brief_Summary_Spiritual: This is a profound summary of Jiva-tattva (the science of the soul). The soul is completely free from the 'sad-vikara' (six bodily changes). Because it has no birth, it has no history, no aging, and no death. It is primeval and ever-existing, making lamentation for the physical shell entirely illogical.
Brief_Summary_Psychological: This verse establishes an unshakable 'core identity.' When trauma or aging drastically alters a person's physical body or life circumstances, they often suffer a crisis of identity. By internalizing that the true self is 'kutastha' (steady and unchanging) and immune to physical degradation, an individual can maintain profound psychological resilience in the face of aging, disease, or death.
